title: 9 Ways To Be A Smarter, Mentally Sharper Teacher
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that mental acuity is an overlooked prerequisite for effective classroom management and lays out nine habits — sleep, diet, exercise, mental rehearsal, focus, listening, saying no, reading, and arriving early — that sharpen a teacher's daily performance. Each is tied to a specific cognitive or behavioral payoff: enough sleep protects willpower and mood, exercise improves memory and anxiety control, visualizing the day ahead builds decisiveness, and declining optional obligations like gossip protects limited capacity for the job itself. He frames these not as an all-or-nothing overhaul but as incremental improvements — starting with just a few minutes of better sleep, reading, or exercise — that compound into greater teaching excellence, arguing that raising personal standards is what ultimately raises the standards a teacher can hold students to.
points: A lack of sleep is described as impairing memory, mood, and the discipline needed for consistent classroom management.
Mentally rehearsing the day ahead — visualizing following the classroom management plan — is recommended to build decisiveness and confidence.
Declining optional obligations like staff-lounge gossip protects a teacher's limited capacity for their actual job.
Getting to work early rather than staying late is recommended because morning is the teacher's mental peak for efficient decisions.
The suggested approach is incremental — adopting just a couple of the nine habits, starting small, rather than an all-or-nothing overhaul.
quotes: Mental acuity is an often-overlooked aspect of good teaching and absolutely essential for effective classroom management.
You need at least seven hours of sleep , and preferably more. Otherwise, you won’t have the willpower and clarity needed to consistently manage your class.
Focus is a constant awareness of your immediate objective and being fully present in the moment . So lock in.
Listening is a superpower that gives you so much more insight and empathy than the average teacher. It allows you to predict, understand, and always know just what to say.
You’re at your mental peak first thing in the morning and will make better and more efficient decisions than in the afternoon.
You don’t have to embrace every suggestion above. Just a handful, or even two or three, can make a big difference. The key is to start slow.
